parts.title: Campus Conversation: Signing Up for the Gym
script: Listen to a conversation between a student and a staff member at the campus recreation center.
Hi. Welcome to the recreation center. How can I help you?
Hi. I want to sign up for the gym. Is that possible?
Of course. Are you a student here?
Yes. I'm a first-year student. I just got my student ID last week.
Perfect. With a student ID, the gym is free. You just need to fill out this short form.
Free? That's great! I thought I had to pay.
No, students don't pay. Only teachers and people from outside the university pay a fee.
OK. What do I write on the form?
Just your name, student ID number, and a phone number. Then bring the form and your ID to the front desk.
I can do that now. Also, what are the hours? I have morning classes.
We open at six in the morning and close at ten at night on weekdays. On weekends we open at eight and close at eight.
Six in the morning is early enough for me. Do you have yoga classes?
Yes. Beginner yoga is on Mondays and Wednesdays at five in the afternoon. You don't need to sign up ahead of time. Just come.
Wonderful. I'll fill out the form and come back with my ID. Thanks!

parts.title: Academic Lecture: Why Is the Sky Blue?
script: Listen to part of a lecture in a science class.
Good morning. Look outside the window. The sky is blue today. But why is it blue? Why isn't it green or purple? That is our question for today.
First, remember that sunlight looks white, but white light is really made of many colors. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet are all in sunlight. You can see these colors in a rainbow.
When sunlight comes into Earth's atmosphere, it hits tiny bits of air. The air is full of very small molecules. These molecules send the light in many directions. Scientists call this scattering.

Here is the important part. Blue light scatters more than red light. Blue light has a shorter wavelength, so the tiny air molecules push it around easily. Red light has a longer wavelength, so it mostly goes straight through.
So when you look up at the sky during the day, you see the blue light that was scattered all around. That is why the sky looks blue.

What about sunrise and sunset? Then the sky often looks red or orange. Why? Because at those times, the sun is low. Sunlight travels through more air. Most of the blue light is scattered away before it reaches your eyes. The red and orange light is left, so that is what you see.
One more thing. On the Moon there is almost no air. So there is no scattering. That is why the sky on the Moon looks black, even in the daytime.
Next time we will talk about rainbows and how they show all the colors in sunlight. For now, remember: blue sky means blue light is scattered by air.
